Measurements of the gravitational constant G disagree with each other far more than their stated uncertainties allow. Recent experiments using torsion balances, atom interferometers, and pendulum methods have produced values that differ in the fourth significant digit, a spread of about 500 parts per million. Because gravity is the weakest of the fundamental forces, the signal is tiny compared with systematic effects such as thermal drift, magnetic coupling, and uncertainty in the mass and position of the test bodies. Each experiment controls these differently, and no single source of error has been found that would account for the discrepancy. Some researchers suspect an unrecognized common effect; others argue that the underestimated uncertainties are simply the nature of an extremely hard measurement. Resolving the problem will probably require independent methods with different vulnerabilities.
